chunks: "In principle SPI doesn't limit the number of slaves, because there's no addressing: the master picks a slave with a chip-select line, so the real limit is how many chip-selects I can generate and whether the bus still works electrically.
The straightforward way is one CS per slave. SCLK, MOSI and MISO are shared, and each slave gets its own CS from a GPIO.
That costs 3 plus N pins, so ten slaves take thirteen pins. If I'm short on pins I have two main tricks.
One is a decoder, like a 3-to-8 on the CS lines: three GPIOs select any of eight slaves, and I need to make sure only one CS is ever low and that the outputs idle high.
Or I use a GPIO expander.

The other trick is daisy-chaining, if the slaves support it: the chips are in series, MOSI goes into the first, each slave's output feeds the next, the last one returns on MISO, and they all share a single CS.
That's four wires for any number of devices, at the cost of shifting everyone's data every time.
The electrical limits come in as the bus grows: more loads on SCLK and MISO, more capacitance and stubs, so I might have to lower the clock or add buffers.
The other trap is MISO: every unselected slave must tri-state its output, otherwise it fights the selected one.
And devices with different SPI modes or max clock can share the bus as long as I reconfigure the mode between transactions."
